questions.question: An $M/G/1$ queue with Poisson arrivals at rate $\lambda$ and load $\rho<1$ is run under an $N$-policy with integer threshold $N\geq2$. Which description of when the server is switched on and off is correct?
options: It stops after every $N$ completed services and restarts as soon as one new job arrives.
It switches off when the system empties, switches on once $N$ jobs are present, then serves until empty.
It serves exactly $N$ jobs per run and leaves jobs that arrived during the run for the next run.
It switches off when the system empties and switches back on after a fixed time of $N/\lambda$.

questions.question: An $M/G/1$ queue with load $\rho<1$ runs an $N$-policy with setup cost $K>0$ and holding cost $h>0$. The threshold is raised from $N=2$ to $N=5$, with $\lambda$ and the service-time distribution unchanged. What happens in the long run?
options: Fewer setups per unit time, and the server's utilisation drops below $\rho$.
Fewer setups per unit time, and shorter queues since jobs are served in larger runs.
Fewer setups per unit time, while on average more jobs are present in the system.
The same number of setups per unit time, but longer runs per setup.

questions.question: An $M/G/1$ queue with load $\rho<1$ runs an $N$-policy with setup cost $K=0$ and holding cost $h>0$ per job per unit time. Which threshold $N\geq1$ minimises the long-run average cost, and why?
options: $N=1$: with free setups, holding jobs back only adds holding cost.
Every $N$ costs the same: without a setup cost, $N$ plays no role.
$N=2$: pairing jobs halves the switch-ons at no extra holding cost.
A large $N$: long runs keep the server busy and shorten the queue.

questions.question: Under an $N$-policy for an $M/G/1$ queue with Poisson arrivals at rate $\lambda$ and service times $S$, the expected time $T(q)$ to empty the system once the server starts on the first of $q$ jobs present satisfies $T(q)=\mathbb{E}[S]+\mathbb{E}[T(q+Y-1)]$ with $T(0)=0$. What is $Y$?
options: The number of jobs still waiting in queue at the moment the server switches on.
The total number of services needed to empty the system starting from $q$ jobs.
The number of arrivals during the build-up phase, before the server switches on.
The number of arrivals during the first service of the clearing phase.

questions.question: An $M/G/1$ queue with load $\rho=\lambda\mathbb{E}[S]<1$ is run under an $N$-policy. How does the threshold $N$ affect rate stability, that is, whether the long-run departure rate equals the arrival rate $\lambda$?
options: Only for $N<1/(1-\rho)$; a larger threshold lets the backlog grow without bound.
Rate stable for every $N$: the threshold shifts when work is done, not how much.
A larger $N$ raises the departure rate above $\lambda$ through longer busy runs.
Only for $N=1$, since idling while jobs wait permanently loses server capacity.

questions.question: An $M/G/1$ queue under an $N$-policy has Poisson arrivals at rate $\lambda=2$ jobs per hour and mean service time $\mathbb{E}[S]=0.3$ hour. The server switches on with $q=5$ jobs present and serves until the system is empty. What is the expected length $T(5)$ of this clearing phase?
options: $1.5$ hours
$0.75$ hours
$3.75$ hours
$9.375$ hours

questions.question: Under an $N$-policy with $N=5$, the server is off from the moment the system becomes empty until the fifth job arrives. Arrivals are Poisson with rate $\lambda=4$ jobs per hour, and each job in the system costs $h=3$ per hour. What is the expected holding cost incurred during this build-up phase?

An $M/G/1$ queue has Poisson arrivals at rate $\lambda=2$ jobs per hour and $\mathbb{E}[S]=0.2$ hour, and runs an $N$-policy with setup cost $K=20$ and holding cost $h=1$ per job per hour. Treating $N$ as continuous, what is the cost-minimising threshold $N^*$?
options: $\sqrt{80}\approx8.9$
$\sqrt{32}\approx5.7$
$\sqrt{24}\approx4.9$
$\sqrt{48}\approx6.9$

questions.question: An $M/G/1$ queue has Poisson arrivals at rate $\lambda=3$ jobs per hour and $\mathbb{E}[S]=0.2$ hour, and runs an $N$-policy with $N=4$. What long-run fraction of time is the server switched off?
options: $\approx0.727$

questions.question: An $M/G/1$ queue has Poisson arrivals at rate $\lambda=5$ jobs per hour and $\mathbb{E}[S]=0.12$ hour, and runs an $N$-policy with $N=3$ and setup cost $K=30$ per switch-on. What is the long-run setup cost per hour?
options: $50$ per hour
$31.25$ per hour
$20$ per hour
$30$ per hour

questions.question: For an $N$-policy on an $M/G/1$ queue with fixed $\lambda$ and $\mathbb{E}[S]$ (so fixed $\rho<1$), setup cost $K>0$ and holding cost $h>0$, the service times change from deterministic ($C_s^2=0$) to exponential ($C_s^2=1$). How does the cost-minimising threshold $N^*$ change?
options: It falls: more variable service lengthens queues, so smaller batches are preferred.
It rises: more variable service is best absorbed by fewer and longer runs.
It scales by $\sqrt{1+C_s^2}$, as variability acts like an extra setup cost.
It stays the same: $C_s^2$ enters only a cost term that does not contain $N$.

questions.question: An $M/G/1$ queue with load $\rho<1$ runs an $N$-policy with $N=1$, setup cost $K=0$ and holding cost $h=1$ per job per unit time. Which quantity equals the long-run average cost per unit time?
options: The mean number of jobs in the system, $\mathbb{E}[L]$, of the ordinary $M/G/1$ queue.
The mean waiting time in queue, $\mathbb{E}[W]$, of the ordinary $M/G/1$ queue.
The mean number of jobs waiting in queue, excluding the job in service.
The utilisation $\rho$, the fraction of time a job is in service.

questions.question: In an $M/G/1$ queue with load $\rho<1$ and mean busy period $\mathbb{E}[U]=\mathbb{E}[S]/(1-\rho)$, the server switches on with $q$ jobs present and serves until the system is empty. Which argument shows that the expected clearing time is $T(q)=q\,\mathbb{E}[U]$?
options: Each of the $q$ jobs waits on average one busy period before its own service starts.
The first job starts a busy period, and each of the other $q-1$ jobs adds one service time.
Each job, with the arrivals during its service and their successors, clears like one busy period.
Each service is stretched by the factor $1/(1-\rho)$ because the server slows down under load.

questions.question: An $N$-policy $M/G/1$ queue has $\lambda=3$ jobs per hour, $\mathbb{E}[S]=0.2$ hour and holding cost $h=2$ per job per hour. In its long-run average cost, the only term that depends on $C_s^2$ is $h\lambda\mathbb{E}[W]$, with $\mathbb{E}[W]$ the ordinary $M/G/1$ mean waiting time in queue. By how much does this term rise when $C_s^2$ rises from $0.5$ to $1$?
options: $0.15$ per hour
$0.45$ per hour
$1.8$ per hour
$0.9$ per hour

questions.question: Under an $N$-policy with $N=3$, the server switches on at time $0$ with $3$ jobs present. Every service takes exactly $1$ hour, and the only further arrivals occur at times $0.5$, $2.5$ and $6$. At what time does the server next switch off?
options: At time $3$
At time $4$
At time $7$
At time $5$

questions.question: An $M/G/1$ queue with $\lambda=10$ jobs per hour and $\mathbb{E}[S]=0.05$ hour runs an $N$-policy with setup cost $K=5$ and holding cost $h=2$ per job per hour. By how much does the long-run average cost per hour change when $N$ is raised from $4$ to $5$?

For an $N$-policy on an $M/G/1$ queue with $\rho<1$, the long-run average cost is computed as the expected cost per cycle divided by the expected cycle length, where a cycle starts each time the server switches off. Which fact justifies this ratio?
options: Every cycle has the same deterministic length $C(N)$, so dividing a cycle's cost by $C(N)$ is exact.
Each cycle starts with an empty system and memoryless Poisson arrivals, so cycles are iid.
By Adam's law, the mean of the per-cycle ratio cost/length equals the ratio of the means.
Cycles are iid only for deterministic service, so the ratio is exact only for $M/D/1$.

questions.question: For an $N$-policy $M/G/1$ queue with fixed $\mathbb{E}[S]$, $K>0$ and $h>0$, the arrival rate $\lambda$ is raised while $\rho=\lambda\mathbb{E}[S]$ stays below $1$. How does the continuous optimum $N^*=\sqrt{2\lambda(1-\rho)K/h}$ respond?
options: It always rises, because more arrivals per hour justify larger batches per setup.
It always falls, because a higher load leaves less idle time in which to batch jobs.
It stays the same, because the changes in $\lambda$ and $1-\rho$ cancel each other.
It rises while $\rho<\tfrac{1}{2}$ and falls once $\rho$ exceeds $\tfrac{1}{2}$.

questions.question: An $M/G/1$ queue under an $N$-policy with $N=3$ has Poisson arrivals at rate $\lambda=2$ jobs per hour and mean service time $\mathbb{E}[S]=0.5$ hour, with finite $\mathbb{E}[S^2]$. What is the expected clearing time $T(3)$, from switch-on with $3$ jobs present until the system is empty?
options: It is infinite, because here $\rho=1$.
$T(3)=1.5$ hours, three services.
$T(3)=3$ hours, as $3\mathbb{E}[S](1+\rho)$.
It is infinite, because here $\rho=4$.

questions.question: An $M/M/1$ queue (exponential service, $C_s^2=1$) has $\lambda=4$ jobs per hour and $\mathbb{E}[S]=0.15$ hour, and runs an $N$-policy with $N=5$. What is the long-run mean sojourn time $\mathbb{E}[J]$ of a job?
options: $3.5$ hours
$1.375$ hours
